entries.note: This is a moral judgment on how OpenAI and Google Brain handled access requests. The underlying facts could be checked, but the judgment itself cannot.

entries.test: Whether Marcus and Davis's published GPT-3 and DALL-E 2 tests were run through access lent by third parties (an anonymous Twitter user, Scott Aaronson) rather than access granted by the companies.
entries.note: The 'pretend to do public science' aside is loaded framing. The checkable core is where their access came from.

entries.test: Whether large language models as of mid-2022 (InstructGPT, PaLM, etc.) still showed failures in the categories the August 2020 Technology Review article listed: biological, physical, social and practical reasoning, object tracking, and non sequiturs.
entries.note: 'So far as I can tell' is an epistemic hedge, not probability language. The claim is vague, but it has a shared reading.
Researchers disagree about what it would mean for a language model to have 'cognitive models of the world', so there is no shared test.

entries.test: Published scaling and ablation studies (e.g., GPT-3, InstructGPT, Chinchilla papers) showing whether the 2020–2022 gains came mainly from more training data or from other factors such as instruction tuning and RLHF.
entries.note: The InstructGPT paper credits much of its gain to RLHF rather than to more data, which bears on the 'primarily' part.
Whether a model has 'a genuine causal model of the world' has no agreed test. The 'maybe fewer howlers' clause is hedged.

entries.test: Comparing GPT-3's original answers with InstructGPT's answers across the full set of Technology Review questions, counting improvements, unchanged failures, and regressions.
entries.note: The finding is Davis's, but Marcus states it in his own voice and endorses it.
